verification.note: Unit 13 (Biomolecules) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 10 "BIOMOLECULES", book pp.99-104; the book prints this question on book p.99 as VSAQ 2. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK WORDING: the printed answer spells the reagent "Tollen's"; it is written Tollens' here, after Bernhard Tollens. The book also states the free aldehydic or ketonic group without saying why a ketose passes the test, so the alkaline isomerisation of fructose is added.

steps.why: The class is named after a test, so the definition has to name the two reagents. The visible result of each test is what the examiner recognises, and it also tells a student what the word "reducing" is describing: the sugar is oxidised and the reagent is reduced.
common_mistakes: Naming only one reagent. Both Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution are expected.
Writing that the reagent reduces the sugar. It is the other way round: the sugar reduces the reagent.
steps.memory_tip: Silver mirror with Tollens'; red Cu₂O with Fehling's.
steps.margin_note: Name both reagents. One reagent alone usually earns only part of this mark.

steps.label: Reason and examples

lines.text: Free –CHO or free >C=O group is present

lines: Fructose is a ketose, but in alkali it
changes to an aldose, so it reduces both
steps.why: The free carbonyl group is the reason for the test result, so it belongs in the answer. Fructose is the exception a student has to remember: it is a ketose, and a ketone does not normally reduce Tollens' reagent, but in the alkaline medium of the test fructose isomerises to an aldose and so does reduce it.
common_mistakes: Writing that only aldoses are reducing sugars. Fructose is a ketose and still reduces both reagents.
Leaving out the reason. The mark is for the free –CHO or >C=O group, not for the examples alone.
steps.memory_tip: Free carbonyl group means reducing sugar; fructose still counts.
steps.margin_note: Write the free-group reason in one line. It is the half of this mark that students most often skip.

insider_note: Two reagents and one reason is the whole answer. The reason line, "a free aldehyde or keto group is present", is what separates a full mark from half.
